title: Florence Nightingale
hookLine: a woman who wrote that God had called her to his service becomes the lady with the lamp

cards: "Lo! in that house of misery A lady with a lamp I see."
The American poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote those lines about an Englishwoman working in a military hospital far from home, at Scutari, across the water from Constantinople.
Soldiers lay in long rows, wounded and sick. At night, the story goes, a woman walked the wards with a lamp, checking on them one by one, and men watched for her light to pass.
The poem made her a picture: soft, glowing, quiet. The real woman was tougher than the picture. Her name was Florence Nightingale.

teach.b: In a private note, Nightingale wrote that God had spoken to her and called her to his service. The note didn't say what the service was. She had to find out.
Her family was wealthy and well connected, and nursing, in their world, was not work for a daughter like her. They resisted.
She waited, read, visited hospitals when she could, and trained with a community of Lutheran deaconesses in Germany. The call didn't open a door; it kept her knocking.
When she reached the war hospital, she found dirt, crowding, bad food and bad drains.

teach.h: THE LAMP ON THE NIGHT ROUNDS.
teach.b: She and the nurses with her scrubbed, cooked, wrote letters home for dying men, and made the night rounds Longfellow wrote about. That's the part the poem remembers.
The part it forgets: Nightingale was also a woman with ledgers.
She kept records, counted, and drew charts to show officials that disease, not only battle, was killing soldiers, and she argued for clean water, sewers and better hospitals long after the war.
She helped found a school to train nurses. Her own religious ideas were searching and sometimes unusual, and readers still argue about them.
But the shape is clear enough: a call she believed came from God, answered with a lamp at night and a pen by day.

Some readers hear in it an echo of Isaiah, who hears God ask who will go, and answers, in the King James Bible: "Here am I; send me." Others honor her simply as a founder of modern nursing. Both can stand by the same bed.

how: Some churches remember Florence Nightingale in their calendars, and congregations sometimes pray for nurses and health workers by name during services.

games.q: you're sure God has called you to serve, and you think it means nursing. your family says absolutely not. what do you do?
o: give the idea up for good.
wait, read, and train wherever you can until a door opens.
games.why: Nightingale waited, visited hospitals and trained with deaconesses in Germany. the call didn't open the door. it kept her knocking.

practice: Bring to mind a nurse who cared for you or someone you love: at a birth, after a fall, in a school office with an ice pack. Remember one thing they did, a blanket, a joke, a steady voice, and hold it a moment.
If you pray, give thanks for them by name, or by face; if not, just let the thanks be felt.
